soil-chem-120.title: Redoximorphic features: colors that record wet and dry
soil-chem-120.text: Soil keeps a diary of its wetness in color. Redoximorphic features are color patterns from the loss or gain of pigment against the matrix color. They form by oxidation and reduction of iron or manganese and their movement, or a matrix color is set by ferrous iron. A pattern counts as redoximorphic only once the processes that formed it are known or inferred. Reducing conditions give disrupted color with complex mottled patterns and points of color concentration, whereas aerobic conditions give uniform or gradual changes. As a wet soil dries and oxygen returns, reduced iron can re-oxidize locally into bright yellow-brown mottles. Fluctuating water levels give red and yellow blotches mixed with gray. Continuous strong reduction from long-term waterlogging gives gleyed conditions in dark gray to blue to black. Eh, the voltage measured in a soil, expresses the potential for these reactions. Classification uses the features: Vertisols with aquic conditions and redoximorphic features are Aquerts, and the WRB suffix σ marks permanent saturation without them. They provide critical information for soil interpretation. See also {{ref:soil-chem-118}}, {{ref:soil-found-025}} and {{ref:soil-found-028}}.

soil-chem-229.title: How a solid appears out of solution
soil-chem-229.text: A solid can form out of clear liquid. Precipitation is the formation of a solid, the precipitate, from a liquid solution. Compounds precipitate when their concentration exceeds solubility, that is, when the solution is supersaturated, and precipitation is faster from strongly supersaturated solutions. Supersaturation can arise from temperature change, solvent evaporation or mixing of solvents. Without enough attractive force to aggregate the particles, they stay suspended as a colloid instead of settling. Ageing a fresh precipitate in its solution gives purer, larger recrystallized particles, through Ostwald ripening. The limit is set by {{ref:soil-chem-181}}.

soil-chem-230.title: Activity: the effective concentration of an ion
soil-chem-230.text: Real solutions do not behave as their concentrations suggest. Thermodynamic activity is a measure of the effective concentration of a species in a mixture, so that its chemical potential in a real solution depends on activity as it would on concentration in an ideal one. Activity is dimensionless. Pure solids and liquids take a = 1, and it depends on temperature, pressure, composition and the chosen standard state. The activity coefficient links activity to a measured concentration; near 1, the substance behaves almost ideally. Equilibrium constants should be defined by activities but are often defined by concentrations in practice, as in {{ref:soil-chem-181}}. The activity of a single ion such as Ca2+ cannot be measured, since cations cannot be added without anions. The mean ionic coefficient is measurable and predicted by Debye-Hückel theory in dilute systems. For water as solvent, water activity is the equilibrated relative humidity.

soil-chem-005.title: How fertilizers make soil more acidic
soil-chem-005.text:
Feeding a crop can sour the soil beneath it. Fertilizer-induced acidification is the lowering of soil pH by chemical fertilizers, above all ammonium-based nitrogen and sulfur fertilizers. It is one cause behind {{ref:soil-chem-001}}. Most nitrogen fertilizers acidify, ammonium-based ones most of all: ammonium sulfate, diammonium and monoammonium phosphate, and ammonium nitrate. Urea and compost acidify less. Nitrification of ammonium releases hydrogen ions and nitric acid as byproducts, which keep acidifying the soil.

Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate, do not acidify and can slightly raise pH. Elemental sulfur and iron sulfate can be highly acidifying, while potassium sulfate has no significant effect on pH. Most commercial nitrogen fertilizers are acid forming, but many manures are not.

Generally 4-7 pounds of lime neutralize the acid from each pound of nitrogen applied. Monoculture with chemical fertilization often brings acidification and degradation. Sugarcane monoculture raised acidity, lowered fertility and shifted soil microbes.

soil-chem-215.title: Resistivity and conductivity: how well a material carries current
soil-chem-215.text: Salty soil conducts electricity, which is why conductivity can be used to gauge it. Resistivity and conductivity are two intrinsic properties of a material that measure its ability to conduct electric current, each the reciprocal of the other. Resistivity (ρ) has the SI unit ohm-metre; conductivity (σ) has the SI unit siemens per metre. In a uniform conductor, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, with resistivity as the constant of proportionality. Resistivity and conductivity are intensive properties; resistance and conductance are the matching extensive properties of a specific object. In electrolytes, travelling ions carry the current, so resistivity varies tremendously with concentration. Distilled water is almost an insulator and salt water a reasonable conductor. A metal has high conductivity and low resistivity; glass has the reverse. Resistivity of metals generally rises with temperature, while that of intrinsic semiconductors falls.

soil-chem-216.title: Osmotic pressure: why salty soil starves roots
soil-chem-216.text: Water follows salt. Osmosis happens when solutions of different solute concentration are separated by a selectively permeable membrane. Solvent moves toward the higher-concentration side until osmotic equilibrium. Osmotic pressure is the minimum pressure that must be applied to a solution to stop its pure solvent flowing in. Van 't Hoff related it to solute concentration, Π = i c R T, for low-concentration ideal solutions, so it is a colligative property. In a hypotonic environment a cell takes in water. In plant cells the wall resists, creating turgor pressure that holds herbaceous plants upright and regulates stomata. Reverse osmosis applies pressure above the osmotic pressure to purify water; ocean water is about 27 atm.

soil-chem-212.title: Brønsted–Lowry: acids give protons, bases take them
soil-chem-212.text: In 1923, two chemists working apart reached the same idea. Brønsted in Denmark and Lowry in England proposed that an acid is a proton donor and a base a proton acceptor. When they react, the acid becomes its conjugate base and the base its conjugate acid by exchanging a proton (H+). The theory generalises the Arrhenius theory, and unlike it an acid need not dissociate. Acetic acid donates a proton to water and becomes acetate; water accepts it and becomes the hydronium ion. An acid is only an acid relative to a base. Water is amphoteric, acting as acid or base, and aluminium hydroxide also reacts with both OH− and H+. Metal aqua cations behave as acids in these terms. Lewis theory, from the same year, defines a base as an electron-pair donor and an acid as an electron-pair acceptor, and explains the classification through electronic structure. It underlies {{ref:soil-found-014}}.

soil-chem-213.title: Buffer solutions: why pH resists change
soil-chem-213.text:
A buffer is a solution whose pH changes little on dilution or when a small amount of strong acid or base is added. It works through the equilibrium between a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A−, a pair defined in {{ref:soil-chem-212}}. Added acid shifts the equilibrium toward HA (Le Chatelier's principle), so hydrogen ion concentration rises less than expected. Added alkali likewise lowers it by less than expected. The buffer region lies at pH = pKa ± 1, centred where [HA] = [A−]; once the acid is more than 95% deprotonated, pH rises rapidly.

Buffer capacity measures the strong acid or base needed to change the pH of a given volume by a given amount. It is highest when a large addition produces only a small pH change. Capacity considers a macroscopic change of 1 pH unit, whereas the buffer index considers an infinitesimal change. Polyprotic acids have several pKa values. When successive values differ by less than about 3 their ranges overlap, so citric acid buffers across pH 2.5 to 7.5.

A buffer can be made by mixing an acid with its conjugate base, such as acetic acid with sodium acetate, or by adding strong acid or base to a buffering agent. Cation-exchange capacity is often measured with a buffer solution at a set pH, and fens keep a stable pH through bicarbonate buffering. For the soil quantity being held steady, see {{ref:soil-found-014}}.

soil-chem-217.title: How organic matter adds to a soil's CEC
soil-chem-217.text: In some soils, humus matters more than clay. Well-humified organic matter and clay minerals together supply cation exchange capacity, and the organic share can be estimated from pH and organic matter content. A soil's total CEC, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, is the sum of the CEC due to organic matter and that due to clays. In fine soils with medium to high-CEC clays most of it is clay-based. In sandy loams with little clay, and in southeastern US and tropical soils with low-CEC clays, organic matter may supply most. CEC is expressed as milliequivalents of negative charge per 100 g of soil. As a rule of thumb, for every pH unit above 4.5, organic matter gives 1 me of CEC per 100 g of soil for each percent of organic matter; at pH 6 and 3% organic matter this is 4.5 me/100 g. The pH link reflects {{ref:soil-chem-049}}.

soil-chem-220.title: Managing salty soil where the groundwater is deep
soil-chem-220.text: Without a shallow salty water table, salinity is a problem of drying and leaching. Keeping soil continually moist, as with low-salt drip irrigation plus mulch, stops salt concentrating as the soil dries. Tolerant plants include barley, bermuda grass, oak, rosemary and willow, but only washing salt below the root zone removes it. Poorly draining subsoil may need drainage tiles, which discharge salty water that can harm downstream water. Seawater flooding after storm surges can make soils sodic, treated by gypsum, or lime where the soil is naturally acidic. See {{ref:soil-chem-008}} and {{ref:soil-chem-013}}.

soil-chem-218.title: Copper deficiency in high-pH and organic soils
soil-chem-218.text:
Copper runs short in two kinds of soil: those with high pH and organic soils. It can also be deficient in organic soils with 10-20% or more organic matter. Tomatoes, lettuce, beets, onions and spinach have relatively high copper needs. Copper sulfate and copper chelates correct a deficiency.

Sulfur is a separate matter. Most soil sulfur is in organic matter, so maintaining organic matter usually supplies enough. Deficiency is likelier on acidic sandy soils and cold, dry spring soils with slow mineralization. It is spreading in places as sulfur air pollution from coal falls, while Great Plains irrigation water may supply enough sulfur.

soil-chem-219.title: Reserve acidity: the acid hiding on soil solids
soil-chem-219.text: Almost all of a soil's acid sits in reserve on the solids; only an extremely small amount is active in the soil water. Reserve acidity is that stored acid, held mostly on organic matter and as aluminum. Neutralizing only the acid in the water would need a few handfuls of lime per acre, but raising pH takes tons per acre. As H+ is removed from organic matter new CEC sites appear. As soils acidify, H+ takes over CEC sites and cuts their hold on calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium. Crops differ in what they need. Alfalfa, from semiarid high-pH regions, needs pH 6.5-6.8 or higher. Most states recommend about 6.8 only for the most sensitive crops and 6.2-6.5 for many clovers. Background is in {{ref:soil-chem-001}} and {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

soil-chem-214.title: Efflorescence: salt crusts on the surface
soil-chem-214.text: The white crust on old brick is the same thing as the white crust on a dry field. Efflorescence is the migration of a salt to the surface of a porous material, where it forms a coating. Water dissolves a salt held inside, carries it to the surface and evaporates, leaving the coating. It occurs in natural and built environments. In primary efflorescence the water is the invader and the salt was already inside. In secondary efflorescence salt from outside is carried in solution into the material. Salt crystals can clog pores and destroy the material through internal water pressure, as in the spalling of brick.

soil-bio-012.title: Actinomycetes: the branching bacteria behind earthy smell
soil-bio-012.text:
The sweet, earthy smell of healthy soil comes from volatile metabolites of actinomycetes. These are soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota (formerly Actinobacteria), Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, many of which grow fungus-like branching mycelia. The order name Actinomycetales recalls that they were long thought to be fungi. Fungi play a similar role, but these bacteria are much smaller and likely fill a different niche. The phylum is one of the dominant bacterial groups, and among {{ref:soil-bio-002}} it includes Streptomyces, one of the largest bacterial genera. Streptomyces and its relatives are major contributors to the biological buffering of soils.

They decompose the organic matter of dead organisms so plants can take it up anew. They build humus by breaking down cellulose, lignin and arthropod chitin. Lignin is hard for most organisms to break down and often shields cellulose from decomposition, so splitting large lignin molecules into smaller pieces matters. Some, such as Frankia, live symbiotically with plant roots, fixing nitrogen in exchange for some of the plant's sugars.

They need plenty of air and a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, but tolerate dry conditions better than most bacteria and fungi. They also yield many antibiotics, among them streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline, and agricultural compounds such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and plant growth promoters.

soil-bio-271.title: Fungi: the threads that decompose and partner
soil-bio-271.text:
Most fungi grow as thread-like hyphae 2 to 10 micrometres across and up to several centimetres long. They extend at their tips and branch, and their high surface-to-volume ratio suits nutrient extraction and invading substrates. Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants, though they were once classed as plants for their immobile lifestyle. Along with bacteria they are the major decomposers in most terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, so they are central to biogeochemical cycles and food webs.

They also partner with other life; see {{ref:soil-bio-226}}. Over 90% of plant species form mycorrhizal relationships with fungi and depend on them for survival, a symbiosis that dates back at least 400 million years. Lichens pair a fungus with photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria, and some ants cultivate fungi for food and nest structure. Many fungi are plant parasites, such as the rice blast fungus and those causing Dutch elm disease and chestnut blight.

As of 2019 nine major lineages are recognised, including Chytridiomycota, Glomeromycota, Ascomycota and Basidiomycota. The last two form the species-rich Dikarya, with all mushrooms and most plant pathogens.

soil-bio-274.title: Protozoa: single cells that eat bacteria
soil-bio-274.text:
Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes, free-living or parasitic, that feed on organic matter such as other microorganisms or debris. The name is now used loosely for heterotrophic single-celled protists, since Protozoa as a taxon is not monophyletic. Classic examples are Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. They range from about 1 micrometre to several millimetres, and are flagellates, ciliates or amoebae according to how they move. All need a moist habitat, but many survive dry spells as resting cysts; they are common in soils and mosses.

All are heterotrophs, engulfing prey by phagocytosis or taking up dissolved matter by osmotrophy, and some are mixotrophs hosting symbiotic algae. Most reproduce asexually by binary or multiple fission; sexual exchange is generally decoupled from reproduction. In the microbial food web they are the most important bacterivores and mobilise nutrients, passing bacterial and algal production on and solubilising nutrients in microbial biomass. Termite gut flagellates help their host digest wood by breaking down complex sugars. See also {{ref:soil-bio-014}} and {{ref:soil-bio-271}}.
